comments.author: whiteknightonhorse
comments.text: On the seller side, the hard part is the gap between the offer and the payment. An agent can quote "3 GB in Japan", think, and pay a minute later after the wholesale price moved. We honour the quoted price until it expires, then answer with a fresh quote instead of a failure. How does the kit handle an offer that goes stale before payment?

comments.author: alexar76
comments.text: Thanks, this was a real gap, and your question is why it's fixed. Until 17 November the kit kept no quoted price: the price was fixed at order time, and after the wholesaler refused an order over a price change, the node kept its old catalogue for up to 15 minutes, so a new quote could be refused again. It now works the way you describe: Every offer in a quote carries quote_token and price_valid_until (10 minutes by default, QUOTE_TTL_SECONDS ). The token is an HMAC over the offer, the price and the expiry, so the node stores no quotes and a changed token is a 400. Returning current_offer with the 409, so the agent can order without a new quote, is a cleaner step than ours: our expired quote answers with a fresh quote and a list of what changed, and the agent still has to read it and decide. comments.text: Ten minutes: QUOTE_TTL_SECONDS=600 . An operator can set anything from 0 to 86,400 seconds; 0 issues no tokens, and every order then pays the price of the moment. comments.text: A correction to "we have no record". After we posted that, we found one: the node's latest catalogue copy goes into the host's nightly backup. Eighteen copies cover 19 October to 18 November, every few days until 5 November and daily after: 402 wholesale price changes on 377 of about 1,800 plans. They come in batches, not as a drift. hits.title: We found 331 MCP tool-list changes in one week that only moved a date. Each one costs a prompt-cache write

comments.author: paul_irolla_6b5ae261d0224
comments.text: Speaking as the author of Tokenade, tool-list churn is the cost I would flag first: a date that changes in a tool definition is a cache write nobody asked for. Where the date lives matters more than whether it changes.

comments.author: alexar76
comments.text: Thanks, and your question is what started this count. Where it lives is most of the story: 286 of the 331 dates sat in tool descriptions, which invalidate the cache from that tool on, while the same date in a tool result would cost only its own few tokens.
